CycleAnalyzer · retrospective 2025-08-17 · model anchor 2025-07

DM+EM Cycle Monitor

Twenty-four economies read as mean-reverting cycles: where each one sits on the growth × inflation clock, what comes next and when, which cycles are not endangered, who stands apart from the global pack — and what all of it says to play in FX and yield curves.

Retrospective edition 2025-08-17. Information strictly before 00:00 Europe/Warsaw (2025-08-16T22:00:00Z). Monthly observations and their release vintages are separately dated below. Policy snapshots include only decisions already announced and effective. Negative FX funding costs are fully charged; a benign domestic cycle does not make a negative interest differential positive carry.

Reconstructed 2026-11-21 by applying the latest corrected methodology to historical inputs. The edition date identifies the information boundary; this is not a claim that these analyses or trades were published in 2025.

02Mean reversion & distance to danger

Each cycle variable is fit as an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. The projected path (OU decay plus fading momentum) is tested against two thresholds: the inflation-fight line (+1σ) and the recession zone (−1σ). An economy whose path never gets near either is flagged not in danger — the cycle has far to run before it is endangered.

03The context filter — which extremes to fade, which to leave alone

Mean reversion alone is a bad idea. A z-score says a variable is far from equilibrium; it says nothing about whether the forces that created the extreme are done. Every stretch is cross-examined against the prevailing context — leading growth momentum, policy direction, real-rate restrictiveness, the clock heading — and against its own turn evidence:

EARLY TURN — the correction has begun but has retraced only a fraction of the extreme, and the context says the cycle change is coming anyway. The best entry: the top is already in, you ride the rest.
SETUP — still pinned at the extreme, but the leading indicators are deteriorating hard from the top. The counter-movement has not printed yet — position before it does.
TREND INTACT — stretched, but the context still feeds the deviation (an early hiking cycle behind a rich currency). Do not fade: the statistical pull earns zero weight until the context breaks.
LATE — the reversion has mostly happened; the edge is gone.

06FX scorecard

Each currency is scored against the USD as the sum of five engines — carry + cycle + valuation + momentum − penalty. The engines are deliberately built on different sources of return, so the sum is less about magnitude than about agreement: any single engine can be wrong for a year, but a currency where four pull the same way is wrong far less often. Components are scaled to comparable size (each contributes roughly ±0.5 to ±1.5): a total above ≈ +1 is a serious long candidate, anything below ≈ −0.5 is funding-leg material.

The five engines, one by one

Carry

0.25 × policy-rate differential vs USD, clipped ±6pp; positive pickup halved only when inflation gap eats it; negative funding costs fully charged

What it measures
The annualized interest differential you are paid — or pay — just for holding the currency versus USD, before anything moves. It is the only component that accrues to you every day the view is *wrong but not very wrong*.

Where the edge lies
Uncovered interest parity says forwards should price away the differential, so carry should net to zero. Empirically it does not — the forward premium puzzle: high-carry currencies depreciate less, on average, than their forwards imply, so rolling forwards harvests a persistent risk premium. That premium is compensation for crash risk: you collect it in calm regimes and give a slice back in risk-off. The model's refinement is that *nominal* carry which merely compensates for higher inflation is not edge at all — it is the currency's expected depreciation in disguise — hence the haircut when the inflation gap swallows the pickup, and the separate penalty beyond that.

Where it fails
in global vol spikes: carry is a crowded trade and unwinds violently, all pairs at once, regardless of local merit.

Cycle

phase value (Overheating +0.9, Goldilocks +0.6, Stagflation −0.6, Disinflation −0.9) × cycle amplitude (capped 1.5) × 0.5; when the clock's ETA to the next phase ≤ 9 months, half the weight shifts to the *destination* phase

What it measures
Where the economy sits on the clock, and — more importantly — where it is rotating to. Overheating and Goldilocks attract capital: rate expectations climb, equity and credit inflows follow. Stagflation and Disinflation repel it: cuts are coming, growth is going.

Where the edge lies
Markets are good at pricing the central bank's *last* move and bad at pricing the *rotation*. A currency entering Overheating will receive hikes that are not yet in the forwards; one rolling into Disinflation will receive cuts that are not either. The heading blend is deliberate: when rotation is fast you want to own the currency for what the cycle is about to do, not for where it stands. Amplitude scaling keeps direction honest — an economy hovering near the origin of the clock has a direction but no cycle, and direction without amplitude is noise.

Where it fails
when a supply shock masquerades as a cycle phase: oil-shock stagflation is bullish for an oil exporter's currency and bearish for an importer's, and the clock cannot tell them apart.

Valuation

−0.45 × REER deviation from its 10y average (z, clipped ±2.5), multiplied by the context-filter gate: ×1.25 on EARLY TURN, ×1.0 on SETUP, ×0.5 on WATCH, ×0.3 on LATE, ×0 on TREND INTACT

What it measures
How rich or cheap the currency is in *real, trade-weighted* terms — the BIS broad REER against its own decade. Real, so inflation differentials are already netted out; effective, so it measures competitiveness against all partners, not just the dollar.

Where the edge lies
Real exchange rates mean-revert over multi-year horizons through the competitiveness channel: a persistently rich currency erodes exports and the current account until the currency itself gives way, and vice versa. But the half-lives are long, which is exactly why this component is the one the context filter polices hardest: a cheap currency whose central bank is cutting into a slowdown is cheap *for a reason* and earns nothing (TREND INTACT ×0); the same cheapness with the correction already underway and the cycle turning earns a premium (EARLY TURN ×1.25). Valuation is edge only near turning points — the gate is what turns a slow anchor into a timing-aware signal.

Where it fails
when the fair value itself moves: a terms-of-trade regime shift (commodity supercycle, an energy transition) makes the 10-year mean stale, and the model will call 'rich' what is actually a new equilibrium.

Momentum

policy direction: hiking +0.4, on hold 0, cutting −0.4; +0.2 bonus for hiking while inflation momentum is already falling

What it measures
Which way the central bank is actually moving right now — not the level of rates (that is carry) but the direction of travel.

Where the edge lies
Policy cycles persist: hikes cluster, cuts cluster, and the first move is rarely the last, while FX over one-to-six-month horizons follows the *change* in rate differentials more than the level. The bonus case is deliberate and is the strongest single configuration in the stack: a bank hiking while inflation already falls is delivering rising *real* rates — the currency gets the differential and the credibility at once.

Where it fails
at the end of the cycle: the last hike is historically a sell signal, not a buy — the clock and the danger model are the overlays meant to catch the turn this component misses.

Penalty

−0.6 per pp of inflation gap beyond +2pp above target, capped at −3

What it measures
A credibility discount, not a return forecast. Beyond a couple of points above target, inflation stops being an input to carry and becomes the whole story: pass-through accelerates, expectations de-anchor, and the real value of the carry collapses faster than the nominal rate can compensate.

Where the edge lies
The edge here is *avoidance*: the cap at −3 encodes that past a point the right reading is 'uninvestable', not 'great short'. Shorting a 30–40% yielder pays ruinous negative carry, so a broken-credibility currency is excluded from the crosses on *both* sides — you neither hold it for the carry trap nor short it for the bleed. It re-enters the tradable universe only when disinflation is delivered, at which point the (still huge) carry starts counting again.

Where it fails
at the moment of a credible stabilization: the penalty lags the regime change, and the first year of a successful disinflation is historically the best carry trade there is.

How to read the sum

  • The edge is in the agreement structure, not the total. Carry confirmed by cycle and momentum — being paid to hold a currency whose central bank is hiking into an overheating economy — is the strongest configuration in the framework. Carry against cycle (a high yielder rolling into Disinflation, where the coming cuts will eat the differential) is the classic carry trap, and the sum catches it automatically: the cycle term goes negative before the carry term does.
  • A single-engine score is a watchlist item, not a trade. A total driven by valuation alone is precisely the 'mean reversion alone' mistake the context filter exists to block; a total driven by carry alone deserves a credibility check before anything else.
  • Why crosses instead of USD legs. The scores are measured vs USD, but the cleanest expression pairs the strongest long against the weakest credible funder: the dollar — with its own cycle, its own politics — nets out, leaving a relative-cycle position. Its actual policy-rate differential can be positive or negative; forward basis and trading costs also matter.
  • The penalty is a filter, not a signal. A deeply negative penalty (TRY-style) removes the currency from both sides of the book: the carry is uncollectible and the short bleeds. Uninvestable is a verdict too.
Worked example — BRL, this month's top score (+2.67): carry +1.50 from a +10.6pp policy-rate pickup over USD; cycle +0.57 from sitting in Overheating and heading to Stagflation in ~15m; valuation +0.14; momentum +0.60 because BCB is hiking; penalty -0.14. 4 engines pull for it, penalty against. The agreement structure, not any single number, is the trade.

The scorecard

Model crosses — strongest longs against the weakest credible funders (a broken-credibility high-carry currency is excluded from the short leg: shorting 30–40% carry is a bleed, not a hedge):

  • Long BRL / short EUR — edge +4.28. buy BRL, sell EUR via 3m FX forwards (rolled); indicative positive policy-rate differential +13.0pp annualized, before forward basis and costs
  • Long COP / short SEK — edge +2.72. buy COP, sell SEK via 3m FX forwards (rolled); indicative positive policy-rate differential +7.2pp annualized, before forward basis and costs

07What is most interesting to play

Each play states the exact legs to put on and the context check that licenses it — a stretch alone never does.

PLAY 1

United States curve flattener

The United States 10y−policy slope sits at +0.01pp (-1.1σ vs its own history, half-life 30m). The economy is in Overheating, which pushes the slope flatter. The clock turns phase in ~8 months, so the window is now.

How to express it
2s10s flattener in USD: pay 2y swap (or short 2y govvies / front-end futures), receive 10y — DV01-neutral, so the P&L is the slope, not the level.

Context check
stretch -1.1σ, still pinned at the extreme; context score -0.18 → WATCH: stretched, but turn evidence and context are both mixed.

Risk — A new growth or inflation shock can alter the phase, policy path and term premium. The measured slope is 10y minus policy, not an observed 2s10s spread; the 2s10s expression requires separate execution pricing and DV01 sizing.

PLAY 2

Long BRL / short EUR

The widest credible model-score gap is +4.28. Long BRL: carry +1.50, cycle +0.57 (Overheating), valuation +0.14, momentum +0.60, credibility component -0.14. BCB's calendar-based policy stance is hiking. Short EUR: carry -0.59, cycle -0.34 (Disinflation), valuation -0.28, momentum -0.40, credibility component +0.00. ECB's calendar-based policy stance is cutting. The indicative annual policy-rate differential is +13.00pp before forward basis and costs. A negative differential is a funding cost that the cycle/valuation view must overcome. The cross expresses a relative-currency view; the score is a heuristic, not a forecast return.

How to express it
buy BRL, sell EUR via 3m FX forwards (rolled); indicative positive policy-rate differential +13.0pp annualized, before forward basis and costs.

Context check
long leg REER: no meaningful stretch — this leg is not a mean-reversion bet. Short leg REER: no meaningful stretch — this leg is not a mean-reversion bet.

Risk — a global risk-off compresses EM carry crosses regardless of local cycles; the short leg rallies on safe-haven flows.

PLAY 3

The fresh signal: Brazil

BCB is an EARLY HIKER: +1.75pp over 6m while the global pack is easing. This is the 'one fresh signal' class of trade: the model singles out a policy divergence. A trade requires that this divergence is not already reflected in market prices; the monthly inputs do not measure forwards or the distribution of gains and losses.

How to express it
pay 1y–2y BRL swaps (short the front end) and buy BRL vs USD via 3m forwards — the first hiker in an easing world gets both the rate repricing and the flow.

Context check
this is a divergence/momentum trade, not a fade: the fight line is not yet threatened, with inflation momentum -0.3pp over 3m — the context is moving *with* the position, which is what the filter requires when there is no extreme to revert.

Risk — single-meeting risk — one CPI print or one MPC vote can void the divergence; keep it tactical.

PLAY 4

The quiet carry: long MXN, because its cycle is not endangered

Mexico is the model's cleanest 'nothing breaks here' story: the OU projection keeps both the inflation gap and the growth cycle clear of danger thresholds for the whole 36-month horizon (phase: Overheating). When the cycle is far from endangered the positive policy-rate differential offers indicative carry under a benign model path, while FX, duration and surprise risk remain — this is where 'we are ok with credit' applies: local-currency duration and credit both clip coupon while the clock stands still.

How to express it
long MXN vs USD via rolled 3m forwards (carry ≈ +3.4pp over USD), and/or unhedged local-currency 2–5y government bonds — the belly, not the long end, so the position is carry, not a duration view.

Context check
stretch +1.2σ, still pinned at the extreme; context score -0.00 → WATCH: stretched, but turn evidence and context are both mixed.

Risk — the safety is model-projected, not guaranteed; a supply-side inflation shock (energy, food, FX pass-through) is exactly what an OU model cannot see coming.

PLAY 5

The reckoning trade: Japan front-end inflation repricing risk

A central bank holding a negative real rate (-2.8%) with inflation +1.3pp above target and momentum -0.3pp/3m eventually validates the market's fear, not its hope. The trade is in the front end, not the currency: JPY is a second-order long *if* the bank moves, a short if it keeps refusing — so let rates carry the view.

How to express it
pay 2y JPY swap (or short 2y govvies / front-end futures); keep duration elsewhere until the front end reprices the hikes.

Context check
this is a divergence/momentum trade, not a fade: the fight line is not yet threatened, with inflation momentum -0.3pp over 3m — the context is moving *with* the position, which is what the filter requires when there is no extreme to revert.

Risk — the bank may be right — if growth cracks first, inflation dies on its own and paying the front end loses.

08Methodology

Clock
Growth z = OECD composite leading indicator's deviation from 100, scaled by 15y dispersion. Inflation z = CPI y/y minus the central-bank target, scaled likewise. Phase angle θ = atan2(infl, growth); rotation = median monthly Δθ over 9m.
Mean reversion
AR(1)/OU fit per series; expected path blends OU decay with fading 3-month momentum (the realistic rise-then-revert hump). Danger = the projected path crossing +1σ (inflation) or −1σ (growth); safe requires staying 0.6σ clear for 36 months.
Context filter
Every |z| ≥ 0.75 stretch is cross-examined: turn evidence (3m drift back toward the mean, share of the 12m peak already retraced) plus a context score from leading-growth momentum, real-rate restrictiveness, policy direction and the clock heading. Verdicts gate the mean-reversion terms in the trade models: TREND INTACT zeroes them, EARLY TURN boosts them.
Standouts
6m policy change vs universe median (robust MAD z), real-rate gap vs own decade, 3m inflation momentum → early hiker, deliberating hike, cutting into inflation, behind the curve, room to cut.
Data
Explicit historical input matrices only. The reviewed source ledger and country observation dates below govern this edition; the present-day repository cache is not an input.

Historical inputs and timing

Information cutoff: before 17 August 2025, 00:00 Europe/Warsaw (2025-08-16T22:00:00Z). Reconstructed on 2026-11-21 from explicit historical vintages and immutable pre-cutoff archives retrieved from the internet; every input history and its availability bound is listed in the ledger below. Projected paths are model scenarios, not later realised outcomes.

All 24 REER (BIS broad real effective exchange rates) and 17 ten-year yield histories use explicit ALFRED 2025-08-15 (Friday) vintages, including the historical revisions contained in that vintage. Later releases and the present-day statistical histories are not substituted.

Thirteen growth inputs are OECD amplitude-adjusted composite leading indicators from the immutable DBnomics OECD Key Economic Indicators archive (commit de4a42daa0ca, committed 2025-08-15T10:45Z); ten are OECD composite business-confidence percent balances from the business-tendency-survey archive (commit 6944e4cd5e27, committed 2025-07-26T17:33Z), normalized to 100 plus the deviation from each series’ own pre-cutoff average. The model scales growth by its own trailing dispersion, so this proxy matches the amplitude-adjusted confidence index up to centring; it is not a CLI. Norway and New Zealand confidence surveys are quarterly and are repeated across their three reference months; the euro area uses the EA19 aggregate as a proxy against EA20 inflation; Thailand has no growth input. Where no newer archived release is verified before the cutoff, the older observation is used and dated explicitly.

Inflation is headline CPI y/y from the freshest matching-definition archive per economy (BIS WS_LONG_CPI, the model-native source, wins ties; OECD consumer-price and Key-Economic-Indicator archives qualify when fresher). The UK uses CPI, not the OECD’s national CPIH series; India uses the BIS Combined CPI history, not the different OECD India index; Japan, Mexico, Chile and Thailand use BIS where the OECD archives are stale or absent. US CPI is the BLS CPI-U all-items NSA index from the ALFRED 2025-08-15 vintage with a true calendar-month year-on-year change and no filling (latest 2025-07). Australian and New Zealand quarterly CPI is repeated across each quarter’s three months; those points are not independent monthly releases. Verified original national releases published before the cutoff extend the archived history where it ends early: Euro area 2025-07 2% (Eurostat euro indicators, flash HICP estimate, published 2025-08-01); Japan 2025-05 3.5% (Statistics Bureau of Japan, Consumer Price Index (Japan), first release, all items y/y, published 2025-06-20); Japan 2025-06 3.3% (Statistics Bureau of Japan, Consumer Price Index (Japan), first release, all items y/y, published 2025-07-18); Canada 2025-06 1.9% (Statistics Canada, Consumer Price Index (The Daily), first release, all-items 12-month change, published 2025-07-15); India 2025-05 2.82% (MoSPI CPI press release (all-India Combined, provisional), published 2025-06-12); India 2025-06 2.1% (MoSPI CPI press release (all-India Combined, provisional), published 2025-07-14); India 2025-07 1.55% (MoSPI CPI press release (all-India Combined, provisional), published 2025-08-12); Mexico 2025-06 4.32% (INEGI, Índice Nacional de Precios al Consumidor, monthly release, headline annual inflation, published 2025-07-09); Mexico 2025-07 3.51% (INEGI, Índice Nacional de Precios al Consumidor, monthly release, headline annual inflation, published 2025-08-07); South Africa 2025-05 2.8% (Stats SA, Statistical release P0141 Consumer Price Index, headline CPI annual rate, published 2025-06-18); South Africa 2025-06 3% (Stats SA, Statistical release P0141 Consumer Price Index, headline CPI annual rate, published 2025-07-23); Chile 2025-06 4.1% (INE Chile, Boletín Estadístico: Índice de Precios al Consumidor (base anual 2023=100), IPC 12-month variation, published 2025-07-08); Chile 2025-07 4.3% (INE Chile, Boletín Estadístico: Índice de Precios al Consumidor (base anual 2023=100), IPC 12-month variation, published 2025-08-08); Thailand 2025-06 -0.25% (Trade Policy and Strategy Office (Ministry of Commerce), Consumer Price Index (Thailand), first release, headline y/y, published 2025-07-07); Thailand 2025-07 -0.7% (Trade Policy and Strategy Office (Ministry of Commerce), Consumer Price Index (Thailand), first release, headline y/y, published 2025-08-06). They are appended only after the last archived month and never overwrite an archived value. Other newer national releases that were public before the cutoff but are absent from every eligible archive are not inserted — coverage is conservative, so an older observation date does not mean no newer release existed.

Completed policy training ends in 2025-07. Monthly policy histories come from the immutable DBnomics BIS WS_CBPOL archive (commit 33517d02aa63, committed 2025-07-10T21:02Z); month-end values for 2025-06, 2025-07 beyond the archived monthly rows are publicly announced targets corroborated by daily decision histories, not claimed archived BIS statistical vintages. The current effective snapshot is the rate in force on 2025-08-16: decisions announced but not yet effective at the cutoff are excluded. Policy-change comparisons run from that snapshot to exact completed-month anchors (3m: 2025-04, 6m: 2025-01, 12m: 2024-07); the partial current month does not add a completed month on hold. Current-rate snapshots feed stance, context, standouts and FX; their assessed real rates (effective rate minus latest eligible CPI) are compared with unchanged monthly historical medians. Historical real rates and every curve slope keep matched observation months.

Policy instruments differ: US target-range midpoint, euro-area deposit facility, China one-year LPR proxy. Indicative carry is a policy-rate differential, not an executable forward quote. The curve input is the ten-year government yield minus the matched-month policy rate, not a traded 2s10s spread. OU projection horizons start at each fitted series’ last eligible observation and the cycle clock uses each economy’s latest matched growth/inflation month, so ETAs are not countdowns from the edition date. Inherited estimators operate on available observations; where documented gaps occur a step can exceed one calendar month.

Original source observations remain missing (no values are filled): policy/JP: 1999-03, 1999-04, 1999-05, 1999-06, 1999-07, 1999-08 … 110 more through 2016-08; y10/MX: 2001-08, 2001-09, 2001-11, 2007-10, 2008-02, 2008-05 … 58 more through 2025-03.

Inflation benchmarks are the analytical targets publicly known at the cutoff and are held constant through each edition’s historical fit rather than reconstructing past target regimes. The US formal 2% objective refers to PCE inflation and Sweden’s to CPIF, while this model uses headline CPI for both. Switzerland’s 1% is the midpoint of its 0–2% price-stability range; Australia’s 2.5% the midpoint of 2–3%; Thailand’s 2% the midpoint of 1–3%; South Africa’s 4.5% the midpoint of its 3–6% target range. China’s 2% is the government’s annual CPI objective for 2025 (“around 2 percent”, announced 2025-03-05 in the Report on the Work of the Government; it replaced 2024’s “around 3%”), not a formal PBoC inflation target. Türkiye’s 5% is the medium-term goal; Brazil’s 3% is the continuous target in force from January 2025.

Benchmark source: 2025 Report on the Work of the Government, delivered 5 March 2025: main targets include a “CPI increase of around 2 percent”. It is public before this cutoff, so this edition uses it in place of the earlier 3% benchmark.

Effective policy and latest published CPI
